body:
What is Environmental Impact Assessment?

Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is a systematic process used to identify, predict and evaluate the likely environmental effects of a proposed project before major decisions about its implementation are made. It helps decision-makers understand what may change in the surrounding environment, how serious those changes could be, and whether harmful effects can be avoided or reduced.

Consider a proposed industrial plant near a river and a village. The plant may create employment and improve infrastructure, but its construction and operation may also produce dust, noise, wastewater, additional traffic and pressure on local water resources. EIA examines these possible effects before the project begins rather than waiting until pollution or environmental damage has already occurred.

Central purpose: EIA integrates environmental considerations into project planning and decision-making so that development can proceed with better understanding of its likely consequences.

Why is assessment needed before development?

The environment provides resources such as water, land and raw materials. It also performs essential functions, including absorbing some wastes, regulating water flows and supporting living organisms. These functions have limits. When resource extraction or waste generation exceeds the environment's capacity to regenerate or absorb them, degradation may occur.

Some environmental effects are difficult or costly to reverse. For example, destruction of a wetland may remove natural water storage and wildlife habitat. Treating wastewater after a factory begins operation may reduce pollution, but choosing a suitable site and designing an appropriate treatment system before construction can prevent larger problems.

EIA therefore applies a preventive approach. It encourages consideration of environmental risks while project location, design and technology can still be modified.

What does EIA examine?

  • Physical environment: Air, water, soil, land use and noise.
  • Biological environment: Vegetation, wildlife, habitats and ecological relationships.
  • Human environment: Settlements, health, livelihoods and dependence on natural resources.
  • Project alternatives: Other feasible locations, designs or technologies that may cause less harm.
  • Environmental safeguards: Measures to prevent, reduce or manage harmful effects.

Legal foundation of EIA in India

India introduced a general environmental clearance framework through the EIA Notification of 27 January 1994. The principal subsequent framework is the EIA Notification, 2006, issued on 14 September 2006 as S.O. 1533(E), under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The 2006 notification replaced the earlier notification, subject to its saving provisions, and has been amended repeatedly.

Under the 2006 framework, specified projects and activities listed in its Schedule require prior Environmental Clearance (EC). This may apply to new projects and to specified expansions, modernisations or changes in the product mix of existing projects. The applicable sector, capacity threshold, location and other conditions determine whether prior clearance is required.

For covered projects, clearance is required before construction or preparation of land begins, except for securing the land as permitted by the notification. EIA requirements do not automatically apply to every small construction activity or every enterprise in India.

At the content cutoff of 1 November 2026, the EIA Notification, 2006, as amended, remains the principal central notification governing this process. The Ministry's PARIVESH portal published a consolidated version incorporating amendments through July 2026.

EIA, Environmental Clearance and Environmental Management Plan

TermMeaningMain function
EIAAssessment of likely project impactsProvides evidence for a decision
ECRegulatory approval for a covered projectAllows the project subject to applicable conditions
EMPEnvironmental Management PlanSpecifies measures for managing and monitoring impacts

These terms are related but are not interchangeable. An EIA report is a study, not a permission. An Environmental Management Plan forms part of the arrangements for addressing environmental effects. Environmental Clearance is the regulatory decision reached after the applicable assessment and appraisal procedures.

Statutory stages and supporting activities

The EIA Notification, 2006, identifies a maximum of 4 statutory stages in the prior environmental clearance process: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal. Not all stages apply to every project.

Baseline studies, impact prediction, comparison of alternatives and preparation of mitigation measures are essential activities within the assessment process. They are not separately numbered statutory clearance stages under paragraph 7 of the notification.

Prelims focus

  • India's earlier general EIA notification was issued in 1994.
  • The principal subsequent framework is the EIA Notification, 2006, issued on 14 September 2006.
  • The notification operates under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
  • The clearance process specifies a maximum of 4 statutory stages.
  • Trap: EIA is an assessment; EC is a regulatory decision.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 163–171; NCERT, Social and Political Life III, Class 8, Chapter 10, Law and Social Justice, printed pp. 127–130; Ministry of Environment and Forests, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, preamble and paragraphs 2 and 7; MoEFCC, PARIVESH portal, consolidated EIA Notification incorporating amendments through July 2026, listed 23 July 2026; official materials consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Environmental Impact Assessment: Meaning, Purpose and Legal Framework

body:
What is screening?

Screening is the initial examination used to determine the level of environmental assessment required for a project. Under the EIA Notification, 2006, it is specifically a statutory stage for Category B projects. The concerned State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) examines the proposal and determines whether a full EIA report is required, subject to the applicable sector-specific rules and classifications.

The first task is to establish whether the proposed activity falls within the Schedule of the notification and which category applies. The Schedule identifies projects by activity, scale and other relevant conditions. An enterprise's size alone does not establish whether it is Category A, B1 or B2.

Category A and Category B projects

Scheduled projects are broadly classified into Category A and Category B according to the relevant notification provisions and the extent of their potential environmental effects. Certain location-related general conditions may bring an otherwise Category B proposal within central appraisal requirements. The precise applicability of these conditions must be determined from the relevant Schedule entry and amendments.

CategoryExpert examinationClearance authorityEIA requirement
AExpert Appraisal Committee (EAC)MoEFCC, Central GovernmentGenerally requires a full EIA report under the applicable procedure
B1State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC)State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA)Requires an EIA report
B2State-level appraisal under applicable provisionsSEIAADoes not require a full EIA report under the standard B2 procedure

MoEFCC stands for the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The EAC and SEAC are expert appraisal bodies. They examine proposals and give recommendations. The Ministry and the SEIAA are the respective regulatory authorities responsible for clearance decisions.

Difference between B1 and B2

Within Category B, the distinction between B1 and B2 primarily concerns the requirement for a full EIA study. A B1 proposal requires an EIA report, while a B2 proposal ordinarily does not. B1 projects ordinarily require public consultation, subject to specified exemptions; B2 projects are exempt from it.

B2 does not mean automatic permission. Where a B2 project remains within a Schedule entry requiring prior EC, it must still obtain the necessary clearance through the applicable procedure. The absence of a mandatory full EIA report does not remove all environmental scrutiny.

Similarly, Category A projects do not pass through the statutory screening stage used to distinguish B1 from B2. Their classification follows the Schedule and applicable conditions.

Why the stages are not identical for every project

The notification expressly provides that all 4 stages need not apply in every case. For example, specified building, construction and township projects under Schedule item 8 are exempt from public consultation where they contain no Category A projects or activities, while Category B2 projects are exempt from scoping. Some other listed activities also have specific exemptions or procedures.

Therefore, it is incorrect to conclude that every project requiring EC necessarily undergoes screening, full EIA preparation and a public hearing. The correct procedure depends on its category and the applicable notification provisions.

Institutional position as of November 2026

On 13 July 2026, MoEFCC issued S.O. 3862(E), amending the EIA Notification, 2006. Among other institutional changes, the amendment provides a 4-year tenure for the relevant EAC, SEAC and SEIAA arrangements and requires the process for reconstituting a SEIAA to begin 6 months before expiry.

The amendment also introduced provision for a Standing Authority on Environment Impact Assessment (SAEIA) and a Standing Committee on Environment Impact Appraisal (SCEIA) to discharge the functions of a non-functional SEIAA or SEAC, respectively, including when their tenure has expired or their functioning has been stayed by a court. Their interim operation is limited to 6 months, extendable by another 6 months. This replaced the earlier general arrangement for transferring Category B matters to the central level merely because the state bodies were absent.

Prelims focus

  • Screening is a statutory stage only for Category B projects.
  • B1 requires a full EIA report; B2 ordinarily does not.
  • EAC examines Category A proposals; SEAC examines Category B proposals.
  • MoEFCC decides Category A clearance; SEIAA decides Category B clearance.
  • The institutional amendment S.O. 3862(E) is dated 13 July 2026.
  • Trap: Exemption from a full EIA report is not necessarily exemption from Environmental Clearance.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment and Forests, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, paragraphs 2, 4, 5 and 7(i), and the Schedule, subject to subsequent amendments; MoEFCC, Gazette Notification S.O. 3862(E), 13 July 2026, amendments to paragraphs 3–5 and Appendix VI; MoEFCC, Gazette Notification S.O. 3863(E), 13 July 2026, standing authority arrangements; MoEFCC, PARIVESH portal, July 2026 consolidated notification listing; consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Scheduled projects split into Category A with central appraisal and Category B with SEAC screening into B1 or B2, with different EIA report requirements.
pictures.caption: The central distinction is between Category A and Category B, followed by the B1–B2 assessment requirement.

title: Screening, Project Categories and Environmental Clearance Authorities

body:
Scoping determines what must be studied

After the relevant initial classification, projects requiring a full EIA study normally proceed to scoping. Scoping identifies the environmental questions that the assessment must answer. It prevents the study from concentrating on minor matters while overlooking important local risks.

Under the EIA Notification, 2006, the Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) determines the scope for relevant Category A projects, while the State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) performs this function for Category B1 projects.

The outcome is a set of Terms of Reference (ToR). These specify the principal environmental issues, information and studies that must be addressed in the EIA report.

Terms of Reference: The approved requirements that define what an EIA study must examine. ToR approval is permission to undertake the specified assessment; it is not Environmental Clearance for constructing or operating the project.

What might the ToR require?

For an industrial proposal near a river, the ToR may require examination of:

  • Existing river-water quality and the potential effect of wastewater discharge.
  • Air quality, likely emissions and nearby settlements.
  • Noise levels and sensitive locations such as homes and schools.
  • Vegetation, habitats and ecologically sensitive areas.
  • Existing land use, local water requirements and livelihoods.
  • Reasonable alternative sites or technologies and proposed safeguards.

The ToR is project-specific. The environmental questions for a highway through agricultural land will differ from those for an industrial facility near a coastal settlement.

Not every Category B project requires formal scoping. The original 2006 notification, for example, exempted projects under Schedule item 8 relating to buildings, construction and townships from scoping; under the amended provisions, Category B2 projects are exempt from scoping.

Baseline studies describe the environment before the project

Baseline environmental information describes existing environmental conditions in and around a proposed project area. It provides the reference point against which predicted changes and future observations can be understood.

A baseline study does not assume that the environment is perfectly clean or undisturbed. A river may already receive agricultural runoff, a road may already generate noise, and groundwater levels may vary with the season. All of these existing conditions matter.

Important baseline components

ComponentExisting conditions examinedWhy they matter
Air and noiseAmbient air quality, existing dust sources and sound levelsIdentify potential exposure of nearby people
WaterSurface water, groundwater, quality and availabilityAssess pollution and water-use risks
Land and soilLand use, soil condition and erosion-prone areasIdentify possible land degradation
EcologyVegetation, habitats and sensitive locationsAssess potential habitat loss or disturbance
PeopleNearby settlements and resource-dependent livelihoodsIdentify potentially affected communities

Why time and location matter

Environmental conditions are not identical throughout the year. A seasonal stream may carry substantial water during the monsoon but little water during summer. Migratory birds may use an area only during certain months. Air quality may vary with wind, traffic and existing industrial activity.

Consequently, baseline information must be sufficiently representative of the environmental questions specified in the ToR. A brief observation made at one location cannot automatically represent conditions throughout a large project area or across different seasons.

The study also considers sensitive receptors: people, habitats or other environmental features that may be particularly vulnerable to a project's effects. A school near a dusty construction route, a wetland downstream of a proposed discharge point, or a settlement dependent on groundwater illustrates why distance and exposure pathways matter.

Scoping and baseline are different activities

Scoping decides what must be investigated. Baseline assessment establishes the present conditions of the relevant environment. Later, impact prediction estimates how the proposed project may change those conditions.

These activities form a logical sequence, but they answer different questions. The ToR may direct an EIA to examine river-water quality; the baseline study reports existing river-water conditions; impact prediction assesses the likely effect of the proposed project on that water.

Prelims focus

  • Scoping defines the matters to be examined in an EIA study.
  • The outcome of scoping is the Terms of Reference (ToR).
  • EAC determines ToR for relevant Category A projects; SEAC does so for Category B1 projects.
  • Baseline data describe existing environmental conditions before the proposed project changes them.
  • Trap: Approval of ToR is not approval to construct the project.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment and Forests, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, paragraph 7(i), Stage 2, and Appendix III; MoEFCC, Technical EIA Guidance Manual for Induction/Arc/Cupola Furnaces, August 2010, Chapter 4, sections 4.3 and 4.4.2; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 12, Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems, printed pp. 137–140; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 14, Ecosystem, section 14.8; official online materials consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Baseline studies record the existing condition of a site and its surroundings.

pictures.alt: Baseline assessment connects a proposed site with nearby homes, a school, groundwater users, a river and downstream wetland through possible pathways.

title: Scoping, Terms of Reference and Environmental Baseline Studies

body:
Impact prediction estimates what may change

Once the existing environmental conditions are understood, an EIA examines the likely consequences of constructing and operating the proposed project. This activity is called impact prediction.

Prediction differs from baseline assessment. Baseline information describes the present situation; prediction estimates future changes that may result from the project. These estimates are necessarily informed judgments based on available evidence and reasonable assumptions, not guarantees that every future effect will occur exactly as predicted.

Types of environmental impacts

A project may have several kinds of effects. Distinguishing them helps determine what requires attention and which safeguards may be effective.

DistinctionMeaningIllustration
Direct impactResults immediately from a project activityDust generated by excavation
Indirect impactOccurs through a subsequent chain of effectsAdditional traffic contributing to pollution in nearby settlements
Temporary impactExists for a limited periodConstruction noise
Long-term impactContinues for an extended periodPermanent conversion of agricultural land
Beneficial impactProduces a positive effectImproved local infrastructure
Adverse impactProduces a harmful effectContamination of a water source

These classifications can overlap. For example, permanent habitat loss caused directly by construction is both a direct and a long-term adverse impact.

Effects may also differ between the construction phase and the operation phase. During construction, excavation and vehicle movements may increase dust and noise. During operation, the principal concerns may shift to emissions, water use, wastewater and solid waste.

How is the seriousness of an impact evaluated?

Identifying a possible effect is not enough. An EIA must consider whether the effect is likely to be significant. Important considerations include:

  • Magnitude: How large is the predicted change?
  • Extent: How much area or how many receptors may be affected?
  • Duration: Will the effect last briefly or continue for many years?
  • Reversibility: Can the original condition reasonably be restored?
  • Sensitivity: Does the affected location contain vulnerable people, important habitats or scarce resources?
  • Uncertainty: How reliable are the available observations and predictions?

A small change in an already stressed river may be more consequential than a similar change in a less sensitive setting. Significance therefore depends on the nature of both the impact and the receiving environment.

Comparison with the situation without the project

Impact prediction must distinguish between changes likely to occur because of the project and changes that may occur even if the project is not built. The existing baseline is the starting point, while the without-project situation provides a reference for evaluating the proposal.

For example, river pollution may already be increasing because of other activities upstream. An EIA should not attribute all future pollution to one proposed project. At the same time, existing pollution does not justify adding further contamination without examining its consequences.

Why alternatives matter

Analysis of alternatives examines whether a different feasible approach could achieve the project's purpose with fewer harmful effects. Alternatives may concern:

  • Location: Choosing a site farther from a settlement, wetland or sensitive habitat.
  • Route or layout: Changing the alignment of a road or the position of structures.
  • Technology: Selecting equipment or processes that use less water or generate fewer emissions.
  • Design and scale: Adjusting project capacity or incorporating environmental safeguards.
  • No-project alternative: Considering the likely consequences if the proposed development does not proceed.

Alternatives must be evaluated realistically. Moving an industrial facility away from one settlement may reduce local air exposure but may create water or land-use problems elsewhere. The comparison must therefore consider the relevant effects of each feasible choice.

Example: Selecting a road alignment

Suppose a proposed road would pass through a wetland used for seasonal water storage and wildlife habitat. An alternative alignment could avoid the wetland but require a longer route. The EIA compares the likely ecological disturbance, effects on settlements, construction requirements and other relevant consequences. The aim is to identify the environmental implications of the options, not to assume that the shortest route is necessarily the best.

Prediction and alternatives guide mitigation

Impact prediction identifies likely problems, while alternatives reveal opportunities to prevent those problems through better project design. Where significant impacts cannot be avoided through selection or redesign, appropriate mitigation and management measures must be considered.

Prelims focus

  • Baseline assessment concerns existing conditions; impact prediction concerns likely future changes.
  • Environmental impacts may be direct or indirect and beneficial or adverse.
  • Construction-phase and operation-phase impacts may differ.
  • Alternatives include location, technology, design, scale and the no-project option.
  • Trap: A predicted impact is not the same as an observed impact.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment and Forests, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, Appendix III, sections on anticipated environmental impacts, analysis of alternatives and mitigation measures; MoEFCC, Technical EIA Guidance Manual for Induction/Arc/Cupola Furnaces, August 2010, Chapter 4, sections 4.4.3 and 4.7; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164–170; official online materials consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Two possible impact chains link construction excavation to dust and exposure at homes, and operation to wastewater, river-water changes and aquatic life.
pictures.caption: Project activities may produce direct effects and further indirect consequences.

title: Impact Prediction, Evaluation and Comparison of Project Alternatives

body:
What is mitigation?

Mitigation refers to measures taken to prevent, reduce or otherwise address adverse environmental impacts identified during assessment. It connects the findings of an EIA with practical changes in project design, construction and operation.

Mitigation should be considered while a project is being planned. If a proposed site threatens a wetland, changing the site before construction may prevent more damage than attempting to restore the wetland after it has been filled.

The mitigation hierarchy

Environmental management generally gives priority to preventing damage rather than attempting to repair it later. The main approaches can be understood in the following order.

  1. Avoid the impact: Prevent harm by changing the location, route, technology or design. For example, relocate a proposed structure away from an important habitat.
  2. Minimise the impact: Reduce the severity or extent of unavoidable effects. For example, control construction dust and reduce excessive water consumption.
  3. Restore affected conditions: Rehabilitate disturbed areas where restoration is feasible. For example, restore soil cover and vegetation after temporary construction activity.
  4. Address residual impacts: Consider legally applicable compensatory or offset measures for remaining adverse effects that cannot otherwise be adequately avoided or reduced.

The final approach does not mean that every environmental loss can be compensated. Some habitats, water sources or ecological functions are difficult or impossible to replace adequately. Compensation is not a general substitute for prevention or compliance with environmental law.

What is an Environmental Management Plan?

An Environmental Management Plan (EMP) explains how identified environmental risks will be addressed during the relevant phases of a project. It translates assessment findings into specific management measures, responsibilities and monitoring arrangements.

An effective EMP answers practical questions: What action is required? Who is responsible for carrying it out? When must it be implemented? How will its effectiveness be checked? What action is needed if the safeguards do not work as expected?

Examples of management measures

Environmental concernPossible safeguardWhat is checked
Construction dustDust suppression and appropriate handling of construction materialsDust control and nearby air conditions
Industrial wastewaterSuitable collection and treatment before permitted discharge or reuseEffluent quality and compliance
Noise near homesAppropriate equipment controls and restrictions on noisy activitiesNoise levels at sensitive locations
Disturbed landSoil protection and rehabilitation of temporarily affected areasCondition of restored land
Water consumptionWater conservation and reuse where feasibleActual withdrawal and use

The measures required for an individual project depend on its environmental effects, applicable standards and clearance conditions. The examples above illustrate the relationship between a risk and a safeguard; they do not prescribe identical conditions for all projects.

Residual impacts and monitoring

Residual impacts are the effects expected to remain after the proposed mitigation measures have been applied. A project may reduce construction noise without eliminating it completely. EIA evaluates whether the remaining effects are acceptable in light of their severity, location and applicable requirements.

Environmental monitoring involves observing relevant conditions after mitigation measures are implemented. It helps determine whether the project is performing as assessed and whether further corrective action is necessary.

This creates an important distinction: baseline assessment records conditions before the project, while post-clearance monitoring checks conditions and compliance after the project proceeds.

Relationship between the EIA report and EMP

The EIA report explains the likely environmental changes and their significance. The EMP states the measures proposed to manage those changes. A technically detailed impact prediction is of limited practical value if the required safeguards are not implemented.

Assessment identifies the problem; mitigation proposes the response; the EMP organises implementation and monitoring.

Prelims focus

  • Avoidance prevents an impact through project selection or design.
  • Minimisation reduces an impact that cannot be completely avoided.
  • Restoration aims to rehabilitate affected conditions.
  • EMP means Environmental Management Plan.
  • Residual impacts remain after mitigation.
  • Trap: Compensation does not automatically make every adverse impact acceptable.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment and Forests, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, Appendix III, sections on mitigation measures, environmental monitoring and Environmental Management Plan; MoEFCC, Technical EIA Guidance Manual for Induction/Arc/Cupola Furnaces, August 2010, Chapter 4, sections 4.7, 4.8 and 4.13; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 163–174; official online materials consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The mitigation hierarchy prioritises avoiding damage, then minimising effects, restoring conditions and addressing residual impacts; compensation cannot replace prevention.
pictures.caption: Avoidance is preferred before reduction, restoration and measures for residual impacts.

title: Environmental Mitigation and the Environmental Management Plan

body:
Why does public participation matter?

A proposed development may affect people who are not directly involved in planning it. Farmers may depend on groundwater, fishers may depend on a river or coastal area, and residents may be concerned about dust, noise, traffic or waste disposal. These people can provide information about local environmental conditions and explain how the proposed changes may affect their lives.

Public consultation is the stage through which concerns of locally affected persons and others with a plausible interest in the environmental effects of a project are identified and considered. It is intended to improve the information available for assessment and decision-making.

Under the EIA Notification, 2006, public consultation ordinarily applies to Category A and Category B1 projects, subject to specified exemptions.

Public consultation has 2 principal components

  1. Public hearing: A formal opportunity for locally affected persons to express their concerns at or near the proposed project site.
  2. Written responses: Comments from other persons who have a plausible stake in the environmental aspects of the project.

Thus, a public hearing is an important part of public consultation, but the 2 terms are not identical. Public consultation ordinarily includes both the local hearing and the process for receiving relevant written comments.

Who conducts the public hearing?

The public hearing is arranged by the concerned State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) or Union Territory Pollution Control Committee in accordance with the prescribed procedure. In Gujarat, this role is performed by the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB).

The hearing is supervised and presided over by the District Magistrate or an authorised representative not below the rank of Additional District Magistrate, assisted by a representative of the pollution control authority. The District Magistrate may also authorise another district-level officer, or an officer not below the rank of Sub-Divisional Magistrate if the project is confined to one sub-division, to preside.

The project proponent explains the proposed project and its environmental assessment. Participants have an opportunity to seek information and raise concerns. The proceedings and issues raised are recorded and forwarded for consideration in the clearance process.

Institutional distinction: The Pollution Control Board conducts the prescribed public hearing. It does not become the final Environmental Clearance authority merely because it conducts that hearing.

Information must be available before the hearing

The consultation process is intended to allow meaningful participation, not merely to announce that a meeting will take place. The draft EIA report and its summary are therefore made available through the prescribed arrangements.

Appendix IV of the EIA Notification, 2006, requires a summary EIA in English and the local language. For a project in Gujarat, Gujarati is the relevant local language for communicating with Gujarati-speaking communities.

The notification prescribes public announcement of the hearing in a major national daily and a regional vernacular daily, with a minimum notice period of 30 days for public responses before the initial hearing. The notice also identifies where the relevant assessment documents can be examined.

What happens after consultation?

Public consultation is meant to influence assessment and project planning where appropriate. Suppose residents report that a proposed wastewater-discharge location is close to a water source used for irrigation. The proponent must address the material environmental concern, which may require clearer information, changes to safeguards or modification of the proposal.

After consultation, the project proponent addresses the material environmental concerns and makes appropriate changes to the draft EIA and EMP. The final EIA report, or an applicable supplementary report addressing the concerns, is then submitted for appraisal.

Does the public hearing decide whether a project is approved?

No. A public hearing is not itself a vote that grants or refuses Environmental Clearance. It is a procedure for recording and considering environmental concerns. The competent regulatory authority makes the clearance decision after the required appraisal.

However, this does not make public concerns unimportant. The appraisal committee must examine the outcome of public consultation where it is required, including whether relevant issues have been adequately addressed.

When is public consultation not mandatory?

The original EIA Notification, 2006, provides specified exemptions from public consultation. Examples include Category B2 activities, certain modernisation of irrigation projects, specified projects in approved industrial estates or parks, building and construction or township activities under Schedule item 8, and certain projects concerning national defence, security or strategic considerations. The exact applicability of these exemptions must be read with the sector-specific provisions and subsequent amendments.

An exemption from public consultation does not automatically mean that a project is exempt from every environmental approval requirement. It means that the consultation stage is not mandatory in the specified circumstances.

Prelims focus

  • Public consultation ordinarily consists of a public hearing and written responses.
  • The concerned SPCB conducts the prescribed public hearing; in Gujarat, it is the GPCB.
  • The hearing is presided over by the District Magistrate or an authorised representative of at least Additional District Magistrate rank; another authorised district-level officer, or an authorised officer of at least Sub-Divisional Magistrate rank for a project confined to one sub-division, may also preside.
  • Appendix IV prescribes a minimum public notice period of 30 days for the initial hearing.
  • The draft EIA summary is provided in English and the local language.
  • Trap: Public hearing and final Environmental Clearance are different procedures.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment and Forests, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, paragraph 7(i), Stage 3, and Appendix IV, especially sections 2–6 on documents, notice, hearing arrangements and proceedings, subject to amendments; MoEFCC, Technical EIA Guidance Manual for Induction/Arc/Cupola Furnaces, August 2010, Chapter 4, section 4.10; NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, Chapter 8, Environment and Natural Resources, printed pp. 117–120; NCERT, Social and Political Life III, Class 8, Chapter 10, Law and Social Justice, printed pp. 127–130; official online materials consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Local residents can raise environmental concerns during a public hearing.

pictures.caption: Hearing proceedings and written responses inform the final assessment.

title: Public Consultation and Public Hearings in Environmental Assessment

body:
Appraisal is the expert examination of the proposal

Appraisal is the detailed examination of a proposal by the competent expert committee before the regulatory authority decides whether Environmental Clearance should be granted. It is the final statutory stage in the standard 4-stage prior EC process under the EIA Notification, 2006.

For projects requiring a full EIA, the appraisal committee examines the final EIA report, Environmental Management Plan, project documents and the outcome of public consultation wherever that stage applies. For projects that do not require a full EIA or public consultation, appraisal is carried out using the prescribed application documents and other relevant information under the applicable procedure.

What does the appraisal committee examine?

The committee considers whether the assessment adequately describes the project and its environmental setting, identifies important risks, examines relevant alternatives and proposes appropriate safeguards. Where public consultation was required, it also considers whether material concerns have been addressed.

The committee may seek explanations or clarifications from the project proponent. It can recommend either:

  • Grant of prior EC, subject to stipulated terms and environmental conditions; or
  • Rejection of the application, with reasons.

A favourable recommendation does not mean that the expert committee itself issues the final clearance. The competent regulatory authority normally accepts the recommendation; if it disagrees, it must seek the committee's reconsideration with reasons before making its final decision.

Who makes the final clearance decision?

Project categoryAppraisal bodyFinal regulatory authority
Category AExpert Appraisal Committee (EAC)Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Category BState Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC)State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA)

This distinction is important because appraisal is the expert examination, while Environmental Clearance is the resulting regulatory decision. The authority may grant clearance with conditions or reject the application in accordance with the applicable procedure.

Environmental Clearance may contain conditions

When EC is granted, it may impose conditions intended to prevent, control and monitor harmful effects. Depending on the nature of the project, these may concern:

  • Control of air emissions, dust and noise.
  • Treatment or management of wastewater and other wastes.
  • Protection of water resources, vegetation or sensitive locations.
  • Implementation of the approved Environmental Management Plan.
  • Environmental monitoring, reporting and corrective action.
  • Compliance with additional project-specific safeguards.

The exact conditions depend on the project, its assessed impacts and applicable legal requirements. Clearance is therefore not an unconditional statement that the project has no environmental risk.

Post-clearance compliance and monitoring

Prior Environmental Clearance is obtained before a covered project begins the activities for which such clearance is required. Post-clearance compliance concerns the implementation of environmental conditions after clearance is granted.

The project proponent remains responsible for carrying out required measures and providing prescribed compliance information, including half-yearly reports on compliance with EC conditions to the regulatory authority on 1 June and 1 December each year. The regulatory and monitoring arrangements help determine whether the conditions imposed on the project are being followed.

Actual environmental conditions may differ from predictions. Monitoring makes it possible to identify unexpected effects or inadequate safeguards and determine whether corrective action is required.

Baseline data record conditions before implementation. Predictions estimate likely project effects. Post-clearance monitoring checks actual conditions and implementation of safeguards.

Environmental Clearance is not the only possible permission

Prior EC must be distinguished from other permissions that may apply to a project. For example, a covered industry may separately need Consent to Operate under applicable pollution-control laws; Consent to Establish is not separately required where the notified exemption for projects with prior EC applies. A proposal involving forest land, protected areas or coastal regulation may require other relevant approvals.

Environmental Clearance does not automatically replace these other legal requirements. The necessity and sequence of permissions depend on the applicable laws and the nature of the project.

How the EIA process works in Gujarat

For a Category A proposal located in Gujarat, the applicable central process involves appraisal by an EAC and a clearance decision by MoEFCC.

For a Category B proposal under the state-level process, the Gujarat SEAC examines the proposal and makes its recommendation, while the Gujarat SEIAA is the regulatory authority responsible for the clearance decision. When a public hearing is mandatory, the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) conducts the prescribed hearing procedure.

The GPCB also performs pollution-control functions under relevant laws. Its role in conducting a public hearing and its role in administering pollution-control consents should not be confused with the SEIAA's responsibility for the final state-level EC decision.

Verified institutional update

The Ministry issued S.O. 4355(E) on 6 August 2026, constituting the Gujarat State Expert Appraisal Committee for a period of 4 years. This followed the July 2026 amendment to the national EIA framework concerning the tenure and continuity of the state appraisal and clearance institutions.

These are institutional facts effective within the selected content cutoff of 1 November 2026. They do not change the fundamental distinction between expert appraisal, regulatory clearance and Pollution Control Board functions.

The entire process in one sequence

For a project requiring the full assessment process, the sequence begins with examining its Schedule entry and category. Where applicable, scoping determines the ToR. The EIA then develops baseline information, predicts impacts, examines alternatives and proposes mitigation measures through the EMP. Public consultation brings relevant concerns into the final assessment. Expert appraisal follows, and the competent authority decides whether to grant clearance with conditions or reject the application. If clearance is granted, implementation and compliance monitoring remain necessary.

The sequence must be adapted to the project's category and applicable exemptions. Screening applies to Category B; a B2 project ordinarily does not require a full EIA report; and some activities are exempt from public consultation. The process is therefore not identical for every proposal.

Prelims focus

  • Appraisal is expert examination; EC is the regulatory decision.
  • EAC recommends; MoEFCC decides for Category A projects.
  • SEAC recommends; SEIAA decides for Category B projects.
  • GPCB conducts prescribed public hearings in Gujarat.
  • Gujarat SEAC was constituted through S.O. 4355(E), 6 August 2026, for 4 years.
  • Trap: Environmental Clearance does not automatically replace pollution-control consents or other legally required permissions.
